findings.where: Hero, the handwritten 'write to me' margin note (the page's one call to action), at both widths
findings.fault: The page's main action has the least visual weight of anything in the hero. It is a few small handwritten words with a pen stroke under them, set outside the text column on desktop. The headline, the clipped photo and the aqueduct drawing all come first. Because it is in the same hand used for annotations and the pull quote, it reads as a note scribbled in the margin, not as the way to contact Mark. Only the thin red stroke hints that it can be clicked.
findings.who_objects: Staff at a development bank who have decided to get in touch. They look for a clear contact action and may skip a margin doodle. If they miss it they have to go to the nav's 'Contact', which costs them a step on the one task the homepage exists for.

findings.fault: The only working contact route is a bare mailto link, and the email address is not shown anywhere on the page. On a machine with no mail app set up (common for webmail users on a work laptop), clicking it does nothing visible or opens an unconfigured client. The visitor then has no address to copy.
findings.who_objects: An agency officer using webmail on a managed work computer. They click, nothing useful happens, and they cannot find the address to paste into their own mail.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the download row 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge · Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'
findings.fault: The row's closing rule sits on the title's last baseline and runs right across, under the 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF' column too. As a result, you can't tell whether the title's underline means 'link' or is just the table's border. The link is on the title only, but 'PDF', the word that says this is a download, sits in the text that cannot be clicked. On a ruled pad, where every line of text already sits on a feint, the underline can't do its job as a link cue.
findings.who_objects: A reader who wants the lecture PDF. They may click 'PDF' and get nothing, or not see that the title is the download. Angélique would hit the same problem every time she adds a PDF.

findings.fault: It is a button (it replays an animation where it is), but it looks like an underlined text link. That borrows the link's reserved underline, so a visitor expects it to take them to another page.
findings.who_objects: Mark or the founder reviewing the tile. They read it as a link to another page and don't expect the margin note to redraw. If this pattern carries into the site, buttons and links would look the same.
